title: Nepal floods death toll climbs to 1,377; search operations continue for more than 5,000 missing - thehindu.com
description: Nepal floods death toll climbs to 1,377; search operations continue for more than 5,000 missing  thehindu.com
publisher.title: thehindu.com
full_article:
The death toll due to the flash floods in Nepal rose to 1,377 on Thursday (September 10, 2026) as more bodies were recovered from the affected districts, while rescue and search operations continue for more than 5,000 missing people, authorities said.

At least 364 bodies have been recovered from Chitwan district, 228 from Nawalparasi East, 222 from Nawalparasi West and 198 from Nuwakot, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).

Nepal flash floods wash away illusions of clean, easy hydropower

Similarly, 178 bodies have been recovered from Rasuwa, 77 from Gorkha, 70 from Dhading and 38 from Tanahu, it said.

Two flood victims died during treatment in Kathmandu.

The joint command of security personnel has continued search and rescue operations for the missing people, estimated to be 5,130.

Also Read: Nepal flash floods: What caused the devastation?

So far, 13,656 people have been rescued from the flood-affected areas.

The flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal.

ALSO WATCH Watch: What is driving disasters in the Himalayas? C.P. Rajendran explains

The Bhotekoshi River, which flows south from the Himalayan border region, carried the floodwaters downstream, sweeping away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaging hydropower projects.

The disaster also killed at least 43 people on the Chinese side, while more than 500 people remain missing in Tibet, according to Chinese media reports.

title: S. Korea to send 2nd disaster relief team to Nepal as flood response shifts to recovery - The Korea Herald
description: S. Korea to send 2nd disaster relief team to Nepal as flood response shifts to recovery  The Korea Herald
publisher.title: The Korea Herald
full_article:
A man looks at photographs of missing persons outside a morgue in the aftermath of flash floods in Kathmandu on Wednesday. (AFP-Yonhap)

South Korea will send its second overseas emergency relief team to Nepal this week to support the country's shift of its focus from search and rescue to recovery following devastating floods, Seoul's foreign ministry said Thursday.

The eight-member Korea Disaster Relief Team will depart aboard a KC-330 military transport aircraft and arrive in Nepal on Friday, consisting of officials from the ministry, firefighters, Korea International Cooperation Agency personnel and medical staff, according to the ministry.

The team will focus mainly on reconstruction and recovery operations during its seven-day mission, it added.

Nine Koreans -- six employees of Doosan Enerbility Co. and three of Korea South-East Power Co. -- went missing Aug. 26 after massive floods and landslides hit Rasuwa District near the Nepal-Tibet border while they were working at a hydropower plant construction site.

"Nepal has decided to shift its operations from search and rescue to reconstruction and recovery and has asked us to support recovery efforts in the affected areas," ministry spokesperson Park Doo-soon said at a press briefing.

The first 44-member contingent of the KDRT, which was dispatched to Nepal last week, will return home after wrapping up its 10-day search-and-rescue mission.

The KDRT, in cooperation with local authorities and corporate response teams, has conducted intensive searches using drones, helicopters and other advanced equipment, but no signs of the missing people have been found.

"The assessment of search-and-rescue operations found significant constraints due to rugged terrain, weather-related risks and the potential for infectious diseases," a ministry official said.

"Despite difficulties, we will continue search-and-rescue efforts in cooperation with our rapid response team, the South Korean Embassy in Nepal and corporate teams," he added.

The KDRT will also deliver about 4 tons of relief supplies worth 180 million won ($134,208) to the Nepalese side. The supplies were donated by South Korean companies and collected by a South Korean nongovernmental organization, the ministry said.

Families of three missing Korea South-East Power employees opposed the planned conclusion of the first KDRT team's mission, urging authorities to continue ground searches in areas where they believe the workers may have evacuated.

President Lee Jae Myung has instructed officials to listen carefully to the families' opinions and review necessary measures to reflect their wishes as much as possible, according to the presidential office.

"The government understands how anxious and frustrated the families must be. We will listen to their concerns and review measures to respect and reflect their wishes," Park said.

As of Thursday, more than 1,400 people had been killed and over 5,600 remained missing following the disaster, according to foreign media reports. (Yonhap)

SOUTHFIELD, Mich., Sept. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Helping Hand for Relief and Development (HHRD) has launched a $250,000 emergency appeal to provide critical humanitarian assistance to families affected by the catastrophic floods that struck Nepal on August 26.

HHRD is Raising Funds for Nepal Flood Relief

The disaster began when a glacier collapse in the Himalayas triggered a massive surge of water, ice, rock and mud through the Trishuli River system, devastating communities along Nepal's northern border with Tibet. The floods have caused widespread loss of life and left thousands missing, while destroying homes, roads, bridges, and critical infrastructure. Current estimates indicate that the disaster has caused approximately $2.56 billion in damage, with thousands of families displaced and communities struggling to access necessities.

Urgent Needs on the Ground

As search and rescue operations continue, affected families urgently need food, clean drinking water, emergency shelter, hygiene supplies, medical assistance and other essential relief items. Damaged roads and bridges have made reaching many communities difficult, further increasing the urgency of the response. Nepalese authorities have mobilized thousands of security personnel and helicopters for rescue and relief operations, while specialized international assistance has also been brought in to support difficult rescue efforts.

HHRD has been serving vulnerable communities in Nepal since 2015, with ongoing programs supporting orphans, water access, livelihoods, healthcare and seasonal relief. Through its established presence in the country, HHRD is mobilizing resources for this emergency response and working to deliver essential assistance to families affected by the floods.

HHRD is calling on donors, supporters and communities across the United States to help raise $250,000 for Nepal flood relief. Every contribution can help provide families with the essentials they need to survive the immediate crisis and begin rebuilding their lives.

title: Many Christians among the missing and dead after Nepal floods - www.christiantoday.com
description: Many Christians among the missing and dead after Nepal floods  www.christiantoday.com
publisher.title: www.christiantoday.com
full_article:
(Photo: X)

Many Christians are among those killed and still missing as a result of the devastating flood that hit Nepal at the end of August. So far over 900 people are confirmed dead while more than 4,400 are still missing.

Christians, though a small minority in the country, have also been impacted, with dozens killed and many believers and pastors missing, as well as whole churches swept away in the deluge.

One on the ground partner of International Christian Concern said, “Local church leaders are facing severe communication challenges. Electricity, mobile networks, internet connectivity, and road access have been disrupted, making it extremely difficult to gather accurate information.

“It may take several more days to assess the full extent of damage and loss. We as a ministry are keeping a close eye on the situation, looking to assist and bring emergency relief to families affected by the floods.”

According to Nepali Christian Churches UK, churches in Rasuwa and Nuwakot have been hit particularly hard. Leaving aside the damage to the buildings, large portions of the congregations remain unaccounted for.

Christianity in Nepal remains a tiny minority, at around 1.8 per cent of the population. Christian leaders in the country have suggested that, much like in India, the authorities and society at large have taken efforts to act against the faith, which they see as an assault on the nation’s Hindu identity.

Pastors have been arrested, churches attacked and Indian-style anti-conversion laws passed. Attempts have also been made by Hindus to have the country declared an officially Hindu nation.

Despite this, Christianity in Nepal is growing. That 1.8 per cent represents over half a million believers as of the 2021 census. Ten years previously the raw number of Christians in the country was just 375,000 (representing 1.4 per cent of the overall population). The growth is largely due to conversions rather than a higher-than-average birthrate.

title: N.C. South Asian communities rally behind those affected by Nepal flood - The Daily Tar Heel
description: N.C. South Asian communities rally behind those affected by Nepal flood  The Daily Tar Heel
publisher.title: The Daily Tar Heel
full_article:
At 8:37 a.m. on Aug. 26, a massive glacier sheared off a Himalayan peak in Nepal’s Langtang National Park near the Nepal-Tibet border, and the subsequent landslide sent a barrage of ice and debris crashing down into the Trishuli River and Bhote Koshi River valleys. In less than 10 minutes, a wall of floodwater rushed toward the border at Gyirong Port in a sheer force of destruction, turning a once-lively immigration center into a barren, gray mud field.

CCTV footage of the moment the flood hit as people scattered to escape the torrential wave went viral, becoming the way many people all over the world learned of the tragedy. The world watched their screens in horror as people were drowned and buried under mud and wreckage.

As of Tuesday, the Government of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority reports that over 1,350 people are confirmed dead, and around 5,300 remain missing. Over 13,500 people have been rescued, and over 7,000 are injured and currently receiving treatment.

Almost 8,000 miles away, Nepali Americans in North Carolina are feeling the weight of this tragedy and are doing what they can to honor the victims and help from across the globe.

Last Wednesday, the Nepal Center of North Carolina organized a candlelight vigil at the BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir, a Hindu temple in Morrisville. Various community leaders attended the vigil and shared sentiments honoring the victims of the flood and encouraging support for the state’s Nepali community.

Community members shared personal stories about friends and family members they had lost, and organizers from NCNC also shared information about fundraising initiatives.

Prachand Shrestha, who attended the vigil, said he learned of what had happened in his home country the same way that many others had: through social media.

Shrestha, who lives in Morrisville but is originally from Kathmandu, the capital city of Nepal, said he first heard the news when he saw the devastating footage circulating through Facebook. As he watched bridges and houses go down from thousands of miles away, he said his heart started to shake.

For Shrestha, news coverage in the U.S. of the destruction and loss of life is important to bring global attention to Nepal and Tibet, but he said it is also important to show the mental toll the tragedy has taken on the families of the victims so that the world can understand the unimaginable weight of such a tragedy.

“This kind of impact, or the calamities or casualties, are for everyone to consume,” Shrestha said. “When I say consume — to take it inside and introspect the level of calamity.”

Shrestha’s daughter, Avani Shrestha, is co-president of Dedicated to Our Community of North Carolina, a group of elementary, middle and high school students across North Carolina that volunteer and work to raise funds for various community issues. Avani Shrestha, her co-president Hansitha Teluguntla and youth ambassador Agrata Dahal shared DOC NC’s current fundraising initiatives at the vigil, encouraging attendees and community members to donate to the NCNC which will then donate the funds to the Nepali Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

“Even though we’re not there right now, what’s happening there still affects us in North Carolina,” Avani Shrestha said. “Just being aware of that and raising awareness about how these floods have devastated, for probably not only this year but for years later on, and it’s going to take a lot of time and money to rebuild.”

Teluguntla added that she has noticed that the news is largely spreading through word of mouth in the South Asian community, and it is important for people outside of that to speak out as well.

That word of mouth has been powerful in DOC NC’s fundraising efforts. Of their $10,000 goal, they have raised $8,000 and plan to raise more than their original goal if they can. The organization’s leaders said they started by sharing helpful links throughout their community. Now, many young volunteers and their families are selling handmade items such as hair accessories and candles to raise money.

Both Avani Shrestha and Teluguntla said that it is important for all people to help those who are affected by such tragedies as much as possible, even if they are not from the same country.

“You might not be Nepali, but you’re always surrounded by a community who’s somehow connected to them,” Avani Shrestha said. “So it’s more inspiring to donate and advocate for them because there’s been a lot of trouble in Nepal recently.”

Dahal added that there is no such thing as helping too little or too much, and doing what we can is more than enough.

“Especially in today’s society, today’s world, I think we could all use a little more love,” Dahal said. “So just the love and support that people have been sharing and are continuing to share truly will help strengthen Nepal, and Nepal will continue to be as resilient and beautiful as it is.”

Kathmandu (Fides News Agency) – “I have just visited one of the main areas where many people were swept away by the water; among them was a school with 300 students. We are still shocked, and people are traumatized. But we are close to them through prayer and solidarity.” This is what Father Silas Bogati, Apostolic Administrator of the Apostolic Vicariate of Nepal, told Fides upon returning from a humanitarian mission.

“Caritas Nepal has distributed aid in several locations and is running shelters for displaced people, with particular attention to children who have been left alone. These centres welcome all minors affected by the floods,” he reports.

Father Silas Bogati concludes: “We are responding to the emergency and are concretely present alongside those who are suffering and those in need. Alongside material assistance, our mission is to bring consolation.”

Together with the Executive Director of Caritas Nepal, Sr. Cecilia Durga Shrestha, Father Bogati visited the flood-affected areas of Trisuli (Nuwakot) to assess the damage and gain a clearer understanding of the situation of the families affected.

During the visit, they also went to reception centres currently hosting displaced families. Caritas Nepal is currently supporting three reception centres and eight “child-friendly spaces” in Nuwakot, providing essential assistance, shelter and protection to children and families.

Father Bogati and Sr. Durga Shrestha also met with Caritas staff, animators and volunteers, as well as local partners, to assess the situation together and identify the needs and challenges being faced at the centres. The spirit guiding those involved in the humanitarian response, they said, is to “stand alongside the affected families and children, offering them support, care and dignity.”

title: Caritas in Nepal: Food, children and human trafficking among priorities - Vatican News
description: Caritas in Nepal: Food, children and human trafficking among priorities  Vatican News
publisher.title: Vatican News
full_article:
By Daniele Piccini

Caritas organizations around the world are mobilizing to come to the aid of their “sister” organization in Nepal, which is working to address the population’s most immediate needs following the flood that struck the country on August 26, killing more than 1,400 people, leaving more than 5,000 missing, and destroying homes and infrastructure.

Raju Pradhan, a Nepalese humanitarian worker and consultant for Caritas International {"@context": "http://schema.org","@type": "ImageObject","contentUrl": "https://www.vaticannews.va/content/dam/vaticannews/multimedia/2026/settembre/09/qwgverbh.jpg/_jcr_content/renditions/cq5dam.thumbnail.cropped.750.422.jpeg","creditText": "Vatican News","height": "750","width": "422"}

Drawing to help them forget

Caritas Internationalis has been on the ground, working side by side with Caritas Nepal and the Children and Youth Collaborative Network (CYCN). Food, psychological support and the prevention of human trafficking are the priorities.

“With CYCN, we have launched psychological support sessions. We have created safe spaces for them, together with different forms of therapy, such as art therapy. These activities are aimed at children staying in reception centers or temporary shelters identified by local authorities, particularly in an area of Rasuwa District,” explains Raju Pradhan, a Nepalese consultant for Caritas International and a humanitarian worker deployed on the ground.

Highlights 28/08/2026 Caritas Nepal: Situation is difficult but Church working to support people Sister Cecilia Durga Shrestha, Executive Director of Caritas Nepal, speaks to Vatican News about how the Church's local humanitarian outfit is supporting those displaced by the ...

“These children,” the humanitarian worker continues, “have seen family members and loved ones die. They have seen their homes destroyed. As a result, they are suffering from anxiety. Many no longer have anyone to care for them. There are many orphans, and there will probably be many more. Through these therapeutic activities, what we are trying to do is help them take their minds off what has happened and provide them with professional support, so that they can fully confront and overcome the consequences of what they have experienced.”

Caritas workers brave muddy roads to deliver aid to flood-hit villages in Nepal {"@context": "http://schema.org","@type": "ImageObject","contentUrl": "https://www.vaticannews.va/content/dam/vaticannews/multimedia/2026/settembre/09/dsc02247.jpg/_jcr_content/renditions/cq5dam.thumbnail.cropped.750.422.jpeg","creditText": "Vatican News","height": "750","width": "422"}

The danger of human trafficking

Chaotic environments, such as the aftermath of a natural disaster, where hundreds of people are moving around, provide ideal conditions for human traffickers.

“We are planning interventions aimed particularly at girls,” Pradhan points out, “because I believe that, in a situation like this, there is a risk that trafficking-related problems could emerge. That is why we will work with health-center staff and other people affected by the disaster, raising awareness of this risk.

Furthermore, he highlights protection issues, particularly for children and girls. “The reception centers are full of men, women, adults and children: they are all living together in the same place. These are also aspects that we need to take into consideration,” Pradhan says.

The floods have damaged water infrastructure, causing shortages and increasing the risk of contamination of drinking water {"@context": "http://schema.org","@type": "ImageObject","contentUrl": "https://www.vaticannews.va/content/dam/vaticannews/multimedia/2026/settembre/09/dsc02306.jpg/_jcr_content/renditions/cq5dam.thumbnail.cropped.750.422.jpeg","creditText": "Vatican News","height": "750","width": "422"}

Winter is approaching

There are a variety of immediate needs, such as food, as well as medium-term needs, including the arrival of winter and cold temperatures.

“We are supporting community kitchens and providing essential goods to communities,” adds the Caritas International consultant. “We have also prepared winterization kits. Winter will be very harsh in these areas, and temperatures are already falling. People need warm places to live during the winter.”

“Together with Caritas Nepal, we also have a longer-term plan that includes launching both short- and long-term recovery efforts,” Pradhan explains. “We also have a much broader reconstruction program with Caritas Nepal. It includes the construction of temporary education centers and support for some people through temporary housing solutions.”

More than 84,000 people in Nepal are experiencing difficulties accessing drinking water {"@context": "http://schema.org","@type": "ImageObject","contentUrl": "https://www.vaticannews.va/content/dam/vaticannews/multimedia/2026/settembre/09/dsc02315.jpg/_jcr_content/renditions/cq5dam.thumbnail.cropped.750.422.jpeg","creditText": "Vatican News","height": "750","width": "422"}

The sequence of the disaster

The Caritas consultant leaves no doubt about the causes of the disaster.

“It was not caused by the earthquake,” Pradhan clarifies. “In fact, the U.S. Geological Survey, an American geological organization, published a report stating that it was a landslide triggered by the melting glacier. A gigantic mass of earth is believed to have fallen into the lake, causing the flood. It was a glacier-related event, and the earthquake that subsequently caused the landslide was a consequence of this event.”

He confirms that phenomena of this kind are occurring with increasing frequency in the country.

“We are experiencing more and more climate-related events, such as floods and melting glaciers, even though Nepal contributes only around 0.05% of global carbon dioxide emissions and 0.08% of global greenhouse gas emissions,” Pradhan stresses.

“The changes we are facing,” he concludes, “are not limited to disasters, but also affect agriculture, crop losses and drought. Climate change therefore has a significant impact on people’s daily lives and livelihoods.”

A shipment of aid being delivery {"@context": "http://schema.org","@type": "ImageObject","contentUrl": "https://www.vaticannews.va/content/dam/vaticannews/multimedia/2026/settembre/09/dsc02331.jpg/_jcr_content/renditions/cq5dam.thumbnail.cropped.750.422.jpeg","creditText": "Vatican News","height": "750","width": "422"}

Caring together for our common home

“We live in a common home that must be cared for by everyone; otherwise, the poor will increasingly suffer the consequences of what happens,” Pradhan warns. “Nepal contributes only a very small share to the ecological footprint, yet it pays a very heavy price, as often happens to poor countries in general and to Asia.”

This is the ecological and social interpretation Beppe Pedron, Caritas Italiana’s regional coordinator for Asia, offered.

The gravity—and even the symbolic significance—of what has happened is reflected in the fact that the Nepalese government has issued an appeal to the international community.

Beppe Pedron, Caritas Italiana {"@context": "http://schema.org","@type": "ImageObject","contentUrl": "https://www.vaticannews.va/content/dam/vaticannews/multimedia/2026/settembre/09/24.jpg/_jcr_content/renditions/cq5dam.thumbnail.cropped.750.422.jpeg","creditText": "Vatican News","height": "750","width": "422"}

“For the first time, they wanted to send a message to the world, saying that we should not limit ourselves to responding to the emergency, but also work on the underlying causes,” adds the Italian humanitarian worker.

Seven minutes to save lives

If the roof of the world is melting, the fate of glaciers below 8,000 meters (about 26,246 feet) is proportionally worse.

“We know that some glaciers below 8,000 meters have already melted and are continuing to melt,” Pedron says, “The global glacial mass is declining; this has now been demonstrated. In the Himalayan range, there are several glaciers in conditions similar to the one that caused the disaster on August 26, and they could cause similar damage.”

Furthermore, the Caritas Italiana coordinator explains that the exact conditions of the glaciers in Nepal are unclear “because this flood swept away the monitoring and control systems. In any case, it is estimated that seven minutes passed between the moment when this mass of ice and earth fell into the lake, in the Tibet region, and the moment when it reached the first populated areas, causing immense destruction. This is the ‘early warning’ window that can be worked on to ensure people’s safety.”

In a few weeks, Pedron will travel to Nepal, where he will stay for around ten days. Relations between Caritas Italiana and its Nepalese counterpart are close.

“For years, we have worked together on smaller projects,” he shares. “Then, twenty years ago, the earthquake in Nepal provided an opportunity to demonstrate our presence in the Asian country, with financial and operational resources deployed on the ground.”

The partnership has since been strengthened through regular reciprocal visits.

“Between us, there is a twinning relationship, characterized by a special closeness, meetings with Nepalese delegations and projects dedicated to young people. A relationship that,” Pedron concludes, “in an emergency like this, becomes stronger, and the support becomes even more important.”

Nepal Leaders Call for $20M Climate Justice Payment After Deadly Glacial Floods

By Chris Walker

This article was originally published by Truthout

Initial observations of the floods found they were caused by glacial collapse, likely a result of the climate crisis.

Government leaders from Nepal are calling for climate justice in the wake of devastating glacial floods last month that killed 1,300 people and left thousands more missing.

Preliminary investigations into the flooding determined that the disaster was likely due to glacial collapse, a phenomenon that is becoming more frequent and more likely to occur in the future due to the climate crisis. The impact of this specific collapse, which occurred in August, was so significant that it was initially incorrectly identified as an earthquake, registering a 5.2 rating on the Richter scale.

“We are paying the ultimate price for a global crisis we did not create … Support for Nepal should not be seen from an angle of aid or charity, but should be seen from the perspective of climate justice,” Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal told the AFP news agency.

Speaking to The Guardian, Khanal added:

The global community should not see this as one-off disaster; it should be viewed in the context of the changing climate in the Himalayas. We know it is going to be a recurring scenario that more and more communities, not just in Nepal but around the world, will have to face.

In an address to the country, President Ramchandra Paudel made a similar call for a larger response to the climate crisis.

“I make a heartfelt appeal to the international community not only to listen to the voices of ecologically vulnerable countries, including Nepal, but also to take concrete and effective steps to ensure climate justice for them,” Paudel said.

Around 1,300 people have been documented as killed by the floods, according to recent estimates. Another 5,000 remain missing. The country’s leaders are seeking around $20 million from the global community to help respond to the disaster.

Aakriti Dotel, national network coordinator for the Nepalese Youth for Climate Action, also called for a proactive response from the international community.

The floods are a “painful reminder of the growing climate crisis facing Nepal and the Himalayas,” Dotel said. “As our glaciers melt and extreme weather events become increasingly unpredictable, communities living downstream are bearing the devastating consequences.”

“We mourn the lives lost and the livelihoods affected, and call for urgent global climate action,” Dotel added. “There must be stronger support for vulnerable mountain communities, and accountability from those most responsible for the climate crisis.”

Unfortunately, due to the effects of the climate crisis, disasters like these are more likely to happen in the future, experts say.

What happened to communities in Nepal and the surrounding region “is unfortunately the new normal,” said Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz in Austria. “It’s going to get worse from here onwards.”

title: Drones deliver food and remove bodies after Nepal’s flood disaster - Ars Technica
description: Drones deliver food and remove bodies after Nepal’s flood disaster  Ars Technica
publisher.title: Ars Technica
full_article:
Chinese-made drones are airlifting the bodies of flood victims and delivering food to survivors in the aftermath of devastating flash floods on the border of Nepal and China’s Tibetan region.

Nepal’s army has been using four DJI FlyCart 100 drones donated from China to make 10 to 16 aid deliveries each day, according to Reuters. This comes after a partial glacier collapse in the Himalayan mountains unleashed a sudden surge of water, mud, and debris that swept through border crossings, valley communities, and hydropower projects on August 26.

The DJI Flycart 100 Drones come with a 30-meter rope and winch system for picking up and dropping off heavy loads. The website of Chinese drone company DJI describes the drones as being able to carry between 187 and 220 pounds, depending on the battery configuration.

The four Chinese cargo drones being used by the Nepal army are currently hauling about 132 pounds of supplies per trip, Reuters reported. That heavy-lift capability has also allowed the drones to remove human bodies from some flood-stricken areas.

The official death toll in Nepal had risen to 1,369 as of September 9, according to a situation report from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. The Nepal government agency also reported that more than 5,000 people are still missing, including 587 foreign nationals.

The same situation report also mentioned how the drones have helped to distribute 1,591 kilograms of food items across 31 flights. The United Nations is appealing for $20.5 million to help 43,000 people in the aftermath of the flood disaster in Nepal.

Smaller drones have also proven useful in search-and-rescue efforts as Nepal has deployed more than 21,000 police and soldiers to look for survivors. Search teams have occasionally found surviving workers trapped in hydropower tunnels after the floodwaters ripped through both operational hydropower plants and sites under construction.

One drone pilot and filmmaker, Manish Maharjan, told AP News about flying small drones inside hydropower plant tunnels to help search for trapped workers but highlighted the challenges of flying drones through tunnels with many “bends, turns, or zigzags.” Maharjan also described finding some tunnels “filled with mud like toothpaste in a tube.”

The drones carried microphone speakers that allowed rescuers to call out to potential survivors or play music, which helped locate survivors in a few cases, Maharjan said. The Nepal government’s September 9 update described 13,646 people as having been rescued so far.

title: Purdue student organization holds fundraiser to aid Nepal after devastating floods - starcitytv.com
description: Purdue student organization holds fundraiser to aid Nepal after devastating floods  starcitytv.com
publisher.title: starcitytv.com
full_article:
On Purdue’s campus, a fundraiser took place to help the people of Nepal after devastating floods. Some reports say that over 1,000 people have been killed.

“The scenario back home is very devastating. The scale of damage that has done by flood is a lot, actually," Vice President of Nepali Society at Purdue Rojina Thapa said.

The Nepali Society at Purdue organized a fundraiser where donors could try some traditional Nepalis food.

The food was donated by Momo and Beyond.

“Food is a way to bring people together; so, when people join us in our event, they will get to know more about what's happening in Nepal, what's the culture and then what people actually need,” President of the Nepali Society at Purdue Sadhana Chhetri explained.

Chhetri said the money raised by the Nepali Society will be sent directly to Nepal to help rebuild.

“The money is going straight to Government of Nepal, the Prime Minister Disaster Relief Fund. This is a direct platform where people can donate,” Chhetri said.

Both students said they felt putting on this fundraiser was something they had to do as international students.

“In these difficult times, we are just trying to stand with them and at least give a ray of hope to them,” Thapa said

They also said one thing they have noticed is that people have been coming together to try and help.

“Ever since the incident happened, every morning I wake up to news that's very disheartening. By the end of the day, we see people coming together for all this, for the same cause," Chhetri finished.

If you missed their fundraiser and would like to donate money can still be sent to the relief fund.

title: Royal Nepal raised about $7,400 on Labor Day, sends $6,150 to Nepal flood relief - The Alexandria Brief
description: Royal Nepal raised about $7,400 on Labor Day, sends $6,150 to Nepal flood relief  The Alexandria Brief
publisher.title: The Alexandria Brief
full_article:
ALEXANDRIA, Va. - Royal Nepal Restaurant collected about $7,435 during the Labor Day fundraiser it held for flood relief in Nepal and has sent $6,150 to the Nepal Relief Fund, the restaurant said in a video posted Thursday.

The difference between the two figures reflects taxes and other necessary deductions, the restaurant said. It posted a screenshot confirming the transfer.

The Mount Vernon Avenue restaurant, which is normally closed Mondays, opened Sept. 7 and pledged the day's entire sales to relief efforts through the Nepal government's official channels. Its staff volunteered their time.

The restaurant had set a $5,000 goal. In a video posted Wednesday, it thanked everyone who came, donated, volunteered or shared the appeal, and said the day had exceeded that target. Photos and video the restaurant shared from Sept. 7 show a full dining room, with every table occupied.

"The fundraiser was truly successful, and we are so grateful to every single person who came, donated, volunteered, shared the message, and stood with Nepal during this difficult time," the restaurant said.

In Thursday's post, the restaurant said it hopes the money reaches people in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, among the districts hardest hit, and provides safety, shelter and support. It said it hopes government relief organizations will continue to show how the funds are being used to help affected families.

The scale of what they were raising for

The flash floods late last month destroyed roughly 7,500 homes in Nepal and left another 20,000 needing repair, according to the Associated Press, which reported that at least 12 hydropower projects were damaged. More than 1,300 people had been reported dead in Nepal and Tibet as of this week, with about 5,000 still missing.

Nepal's disaster authorities put preliminary damage at $2.56 billion, close to a fifth of the country's roughly $14 billion annual budget, the AP reported. Some estimates of the full rebuilding cost run to $4 billion or $5 billion. The disaster is an early test for a government that took office in March after a year of political upheaval, and Nepal has asked for international help.

Against that, $6,150 from a restaurant on Mount Vernon Avenue is a small sum. It is also a full day's work from a staff that gave it away.

Royal Nepal said it would keep posting updates on the transfer and on how the money is being spent.

The restaurant is at 3807 Mount Vernon Ave.

title: Nepal Flood Death Toll Rises as Aid Needs Soar - International Organization for Migration
description: Nepal Flood Death Toll Rises as Aid Needs Soar  International Organization for Migration
publisher.title: International Organization for Migration
full_article:
Kathmandu/Geneva 8 September 2026 – Humanitarian needs are growing rapidly in Nepal after devastating floods last month affected 84,000 people. The death toll has risen to 1,356 while nearly 4,900 remain missing, according to figures reported on 07 September by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA). Roads, bridges, health facilities, and schools have suffered extensive damage.

As thousands of families struggle with displacement, loss and uncertainty, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) is appealing for USD 20.5 million to assist 43,000 people in support of the Government of Nepal-led response. Aligned with the inter-agency flash appeal launched by the UN and humanitarian partners, IOM's response focuses on strengthening displacement tracking and site coordination, while scaling up shelter, health, and protection assistance for displaced and affected communities.

“For thousands of families, the immediate shock of the floods has been followed by immense uncertainty about their next steps," said Helene Fors, IOM Chief of Mission in Nepal. "Our priority is to ensure that humanitarian action is guided by reliable information and that critical assistance reaches those who need it most.”

IOM teams are already on the ground supporting the response, including in hard-to-reach locations. IOM has conducted initial assessments at holding centres where displaced families are currently residing and has provided critical medicines to health authorities. However, sustained funding is required to expand assistance to affected communities.

Priorities include emergency shelter support, particularly as winter approaches; access to health and psychosocial support services; and targeted protection support for people facing heightened risks, including women, children, older persons, and persons with disabilities.

By expanding the use of its Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), IOM is also helping authorities to track displacement locations and population movements to identify urgent needs so assistance can be directed where it is needed most. As thousands of displaced people shelter in schools, monasteries, public buildings and host communities, IOM will help ensure they can access assistance, services and protection as co-chair of the Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) Cluster, led by the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction (DUDBC).

IOM urges the international community to act now and help ensure that affected communities receive the assistance and protection they need.

title: Lions Clubs International Foundation Awards US$200,000 for Lions-Led Flood Relief in Nepal - GlobeNewswire
description: Lions Clubs International Foundation Awards US$200,000 for Lions-Led Flood Relief in Nepal  GlobeNewswire
publisher.title: GlobeNewswire
full_article:
OAK BROOK, Ill., Sept. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Lions in Nepal are using a US$200,000 Major Catastrophe Grant from Lions Clubs International Foundation (LCIF) to deliver emergency relief and support longer-term recovery following devastating flash floods that have killed more than 1,000 people and left thousands missing.

Triggered by the collapse of glacial ice and rock near the Nepal-China border, the floods swept through communities, destroying homes, roads, schools, bridges and other critical infrastructure. Immediate assistance made possible with the grant funding includes family food packages, as well as drinking water, blankets, sleeping mats, hygiene and sanitation kits, basic clothing, first-aid and essential medical supplies and temporary shelters. Lions will also support rescue operations and help clear flood debris and mud from affected areas. Additionally, they will provide short-term care and rehabilitation assistance for children who have lost parents or other family members in the disaster.

“When disaster strikes, Lions step forward,” said A.P. Singh, chairperson of LCIF. “In the wake of the devastating floods, Lions are coming together to reach people in need, providing relief, supporting affected families and standing beside communities through one of their most difficult moments.”

Because Lions live and serve in these communities, they are well positioned to identify urgent needs, direct resources where they can have the greatest impact and remain engaged as recovery continues. In addition to the LCIF grant, Lions across Nepal raised US$67,000 for relief efforts and Lions in several other countries are adding their financial support. With these resources, local Lions are developing plans to help the region rebuild after immediate needs are met.

“Lions’ service is more than a one-time volunteer activity,” Singh added. “It is a commitment to stand with people when they need us most.”

LCIF Disaster Relief Grants support Lions-led efforts through all phases of disaster response. Since July 1, 2026, LCIF has awarded more than US$1.3 million in disaster relief funding to Lions in regions impacted by natural disasters around the world. To support Lions’ efforts in Nepal and communities affected by future disasters, visit lionsclubs.org/donate or connect with your local Lions club.

About Lions Clubs International Foundation

Lions Clubs International Foundation (LCIF) is the global foundation supporting the 1.4 million members of Lions Clubs International through grant funds that expand their compassionate works and empower their service at home and around the world. Since its founding in 1968, LCIF has awarded more than 25,000 grants totaling more than US$1.3 billion. We improve health and well-being, strengthen communities and support those in need, locally and globally.
